## A laboratory, not a black box

LLM Lab is a hands-on path to understanding modern language models, starting with vectors, probabilities, loss functions, and gradients. The goal is **not** to train a production model from scratch: it is to build small, inspectable components and compare their behavior with trustworthy references.

:::: {.learning-grid}
::: {.learning-card}
<span class="step">00 / FOUNDATIONS</span>

### Numerical foundations

Understand logits, probabilities, cross-entropy, and gradients.

**Outcome:** a loss function and its gradient checked numerically.

[Explore the foundations](https://github.com/JM-Brun/llm-lab/blob/main/docs/mathematical-foundations.md){.card-link}
:::
::: {.learning-card}
<span class="step">01 / DATA</span>

### Text and tokenization

Map text to token IDs and build training windows.

**Outcome:** tested encode/decode behavior and inspectable examples.
:::
::: {.learning-card learning-card-featured}
<span class="step">02 / ATTENTION</span>

### Causal attention

Understand queries, keys, values, and the mask that blocks access to future tokens.

**Outcome:** causal attention with shape and mask tests.

[Read the first chapter](transformer.qmd){.card-link}
:::
::: {.learning-card}
<span class="step">03 / MODEL</span>

### Build a tiny GPT

Connect embeddings, Transformer blocks, next-token prediction, and generation.

**Outcome:** an observable training loop, validation, and generation.
:::
::: {.learning-card}
<span class="step">04 / ADAPTATION</span>

### Fine-tuning and SFT

Establish a baseline, adapt a model to a task, and analyze errors.

**Outcome:** a documented experimental protocol and comparable results.
:::
::: {.learning-card}
<span class="step">05 / EVALUATION</span>

### Efficiency and reliability

Measure quality, memory, and latency trade-offs without overinterpreting one metric.

**Outcome:** ablations, uncertainty estimates, and explicit limitations.
:::
::::

The [detailed learning path](https://github.com/JM-Brun/llm-lab/blob/main/docs/learning-path.md) defines exit criteria for each module. Python implementations live in `src/llm_lab/`; Quarto pages explain the mathematics, show minimal code, and link to executable tests.

## A six-step learning loop

:::: {.method-grid}
::: {.method-step}
<span>01</span>
**Intuition**

Start with a small example and a precise question.
:::
::: {.method-step}
<span>02</span>
**Mathematics**

State equations, dimensions, and assumptions.
:::
::: {.method-step}
<span>03</span>
**Implementation**

Write a readable Python reference implementation.
:::
::: {.method-step}
<span>04</span>
**Tests**

Check numerical properties and edge cases.
:::
::: {.method-step}
<span>05</span>
**Experiment**

Compare against a baseline with controlled data and configuration.
:::
::: {.method-step}
<span>06</span>
**Analysis**

Report results, failures, and limitations.
:::
::::

## First chapter: causal attention

Attention builds a context-aware representation for each token. In an autoregressive model such as GPT, a causal mask prevents a position from using future tokens.

![GPT-2 decoder block stack.](https://jalammar.github.io/images/gpt2/gpt2-transformer-block-vectors-2.png){fig-alt="Stack of decoder blocks with masked self-attention and a feed-forward network" width=100%}

## Beyond default assumptions

Some common assumptions deserve to be tested rather than repeated. These notes connect mathematics, research literature, and reproducible experiments.

:::: {.learning-grid}
::: {.learning-card}
<span class="step">06 / METRICS</span>

### Cosine similarity

When does the angle between two embeddings reflect the similarity we care about? Anisotropy, *hubness*, alternative metrics, and evaluation protocols.

[Read the critical note](cosine-similarity.qmd){.card-link}
:::
::: {.learning-card}
<span class="step">07 / REPRESENTATIONS</span>

### The linearity hypothesis

Distinguish representation, decodability, and causal use; understand XOR, superposition, and the limits of probes.

[Read the critical note](embedding-linearity.qmd){.card-link}
:::
::::

## Follow project progress

The [repository roadmap](../docs/roadmap.md) distinguishes implemented features, priority work, and the acceptance criteria required to mark a module complete. It avoids treating a published explanation as proof that an implementation or experiment has been verified.

## Project principles

:::: {.principle-grid}
::: {.principle}
**Reproducibility**

Fix data, configuration, and random seeds where relevant.
:::
::: {.principle}
**Scientific rigor**

Keep training, validation, and test data separate; avoid single-metric conclusions.
:::
::: {.principle}
**Verification**

Check gradients with finite differences when appropriate.
:::
::: {.principle}
**Provenance**

Cite external work, figures, datasets, and implementations.
:::
